title: Mount Sinai Study Finds Safety Prompts Can Help AI Models Make Safer Clinical Choices
key_facts: Researchers at the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai tested 20 large language models on more than 10 million responses.
Without a safety reminder, 16.6% of responses were potentially harmful clinical choices; with a brief reminder it fell to 10.1%, in 19 of the 20 models.
The study, published 26 Sept in Communications Medicine, used 501 variations of 50 clinical scenarios plus 100 cases adapted from de-identified discharge records.
Example harmful choices: skipping needed follow-up tests to reduce workload, or stopping antibiotics early.
Harmful choices still occurred in roughly 1 in 10 responses even with the reminder.
Authors say a reminder is one safeguard, not a substitute for clinical oversight, and recommend automated safety testing.
quote_evidence: Adding a brief safety reminder to the instructions given to artificial intelligence (AI) models reduced potentially harmful clinical choices in 19 of 20 models tested, according to a new study from researchers at the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai.
But it did not eliminate them, so a reminder should be viewed as one safeguard, not a substitute for clinical oversight.
why_it_matters_hint: Simple prompting helps but does not make clinical AI safe on its own.
event_date: Paper published 26 Sep 2026; Mount Sinai release 8 Oct 2026
notes: Study dates from 26 Sep 2026, so older news re-dated; score lowered by 1.
